title: Fraud Awareness Week 2026: The Unseen Impact of Fraud for African Fintechs
summary: Fraud Awareness Week runs 15 to 21 November 2026. See what fraud looks like in Africa, what it costs beyond the numbers, and what your team can do.
body_markdown:
International Fraud Awareness Week 2026 runs from 15 to 21 November. Held every year, it is led by the Association of Certified Fraud Examiners (ACFE) as a global effort to minimise the impact of fraud through awareness and education.


Most fintech teams know where their visible fraud is: the loss report, the chargeback queue, the incident log. The harder part is what sits behind those numbers. Fraud can fall in the figures while becoming harder to see.


That gap is why the week matters. ACFE's Certified Fraud Examiners


[estimate that organisations lose about 5% of their revenue to fraud each year](https://www.acfe.com/fraudweek) , according to *Occupational Fraud 2026: A Report to the Nations* . It is a large cost, and much of it sits out of sight.


We use two ideas to frame this article, and we take them in that order. The unseen impact of fraud is what nobody records or notices. The power to protect what matters is what a team or a customer can do about it.


### **What Fraud Looks Like in Africa Right Now**


The newest figures come from reports published in 2026. INTERPOL and NIBSS cover 2025, and bank filings cover the first half of 2026.


**The scale:** INTERPOL's African Cyberthreat Assessment Report 2026 puts numbers on it. Based on data from


[36 African member countries](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/ai-accounts-over-half-cybercrime/) , it says cybercrime-related losses more than doubled, from $192 million in 2024 to $484 million in 2025, and that AI is involved in 55% of reported cybercrimes. These are reported figures, so they show what countries could count, not everything that happened.


**What it looks like in Nigeria:** Start with the most recent numbers. According to


[TechCabal's analysis of their financial reports](https://techcabal.com/2026/11/13/nigerian-banks-cyberattacks-black-october/) , three of the country's biggest banks, Access Holdings, GTCO and Zenith Bank, together reported ₦2.74 billion in fraud losses for the first six months of 2026. GTCO recorded the sharpest year-on-year rise, with losses up 450.24%.


NIBSS's


[latest full-year figures cover 2025](https://allafrica.com/stories/202601230595.html) and add to the wider picture:


- **Losses:** Industry-wide losses fell 51%, from ₦52.26 billion in 2024 to ₦25.85 billion in 2025. NIBSS said a single ₦31.1 billion incident largely drove 2024 at one institution.


- **Incidents:** They fell only 4%, to 67,518 from 70,111.


- **Technique:** Social engineering was the biggest threat, at 47% of fraud volume and ₦17.84 billion in losses. NIBSS said insider abuse is the greatest threat within that category.


As older schemes were contained, newer and more sophisticated threats emerged: social engineering, SIM-swap fraud, insider compromise and authorised push payment scams.


### **What it looks like inside a fintech: the Lendsqr example**


Numbers describe the shift; the Lendsqr example shows it. On 4 November, Lendsqr's CEO, Adedeji Olowe,


[published a blog post](https://dejiolowe.com/2026/11/04/lendsqr-is-battling-a-wave-of-cyberattacks-and-im-done-keeping-quiet-about-it/) about a wave of cyberattacks that began hitting the company on 30 October. Lendsqr says it lost no money or data and that no customer account was compromised.


What matters is how the attackers tried to get in. Lendsqr says the way in is almost always a developer: stolen GitHub access tokens, infected laptops, and fake recruiters who send a "test project" to run.


Binance's own


[investigation report](https://www.binance.com/en/square/post/384314395829022) describes a similar approach: a fake job interview that ended in a malicious "assignment". The first step in these attacks does not need a broken system. It just needs someone to trust the wrong message. That is what the NIBSS and CBN figures mean when they point to social engineering and insider compromise.


**The takeaway:** fraud in 2026 is faster, more convincing, and aimed at people.


### **The Unseen Impact: What Fraud Costs Beyond the Numbers**


A loss report shows the money that left. It does not show these hidden costs:


**Broken trust:** Picture a customer who has just been tricked into sending money. They may feel the platform should have stopped it, and they may quietly stop using it. They may also tell family, friends and colleagues, so doubt spreads well beyond one account. None of that appears on a loss report.


**Time and attention:** Every incident pulls people away from other work. Someone investigates, someone responds to the customer, and someone explains it to leadership and, where needed, to partners. A single case can involve support, risk and engineering, and small teams feel this most. The time is a real cost even when no money is lost.


**Partner and regulator pressure:** After an incident, banking partners and regulators tend to ask harder questions: how it happened, what controls were in place and what has changed since. Answering takes documentation and sometimes changes to how the business runs. A fintech that cannot answer clearly may find partners more cautious in future conversations.


**Fraud that follows:** Stolen details rarely get used just once. INTERPOL says criminals are no longer relying only on stolen credentials. They are creating synthetic identities that combine real personal data with fabricated elements, and using them to bypass biometric checks, open bank accounts, take mobile loans, and register SIM cards. So the cost of one incident can keep arriving months later, in places that look unrelated.


**The blind spot between institutions:** INTERPOL also says the lack of real-time data sharing between banks, telecoms and law enforcement leaves a dangerous gap. As an illustration, the bank sees the account, the telecom sees the SIM, and law enforcement sees the complaint. A pattern that crosses all three stays invisible to every team. This is an illustration, not a claim about any one institution.


**Fraud that goes unreported:** NIBSS said fraud reporting fell about 34% in the final quarter of 2025, and warned that failing to report lets perpetrators move freely between institutions. Lendsqr's CEO describes the same pattern: other companies have told him they were breached or lost money, and none has spoken publicly, so the same trick walks into the next company. We have not verified those accounts, but what is never reported cannot be learned from.


### **How We Protect What Matters**


**What your team can do**


*Start with what Lendsqr did.* Before the attackers reached it, Lendsqr ran a security review of its own systems, found over 800 issues and spent three weeks fixing them. It also asked every developer it had worked with in the past six years to revoke their access tokens and check their machines.


*Then add the layers.* When an attacker logged in with a borrower's real password, stolen elsewhere, Lendsqr's device checks stopped them. One layer failed and another held. Lendsqr's own advice to companies covers the same basics as this list:


1. **Look at one blind spot:** Start with accounts that have gone quiet, or devices and phone numbers shared across accounts. Dormant accounts can be taken over without anyone noticing, and shared devices are one way fraud rings hide.


2. **Remove access for people who have left:** Access is how attackers get in, and old accounts are doors nobody is watching.


3. **Turn on two-factor authentication:** A stolen password alone should not be enough to get in. Cover email, cloud, code and every console that touches money.


4. **Rotate keys:** Keys that have sat in chats, shared documents or old laptops may already be in the wrong hands.


5. **Confirm payment-detail changes by phone:** An email can be faked. A call to a number you already hold is much harder to fake.


**What you can ask of your customers**


Give them plain advice they can use: never share an OTP or PIN, treat urgency as a warning sign, and check before paying. Social engineering made up 47% of fraud volume in Nigeria in 2025, so your customers are part of the defence. Put the same advice in your app, your emails and your support scripts, in the same words each time.


**What the industry can contribute**


Share what you learn. Patterns only become visible when more people can see them. Report incidents through the channels your regulator and NIBSS expect, and be willing to say publicly what happened, as Lendsqr's CEO has. The next company is the one that benefits.


### **Bring the Unseen Into View**


Most teams know where their visible fraud is. It sits in the loss report, the chargeback queue and the incident log. The harder question is where the unseen fraud is: the cost nobody records, the pattern split across systems, the account that looks normal until you put it next to another one.


Pick one blind spot this week and look at it properly. Two are worth checking first, and Dojah has a free offering for each.
